blocks.text: What do property managers look for during an inspection

When you walk through a unit, you are checking for three specific categories. First, you look for physical damage beyond normal wear and tear. This includes holes in walls, stained carpets, or broken fixtures. Second, you check for lease compliance. Are there unauthorized pets or extra tenants living in the unit. Third, you document safety hazards. These are things like smoke detector functionality, window lock integrity, and mold growth.

The real work starts when you return to your Mac. You likely have notes in a physical notebook, photos on your iPhone, and a blank template in Microsoft Word. Moving these into a professional format takes hours. You have to rename files, copy text, and format tables. This is where most managers lose time. It is a manual process that invites errors.

items: Data fragmentation across phone, paper, and computer.
Manual entry into spreadsheets or property management software.
Delays in sending reports to owners or maintenance teams.

blocks.text: You do not need new software to start improving your workflow. Standardize your templates. Create a single Google Sheets file that acts as your master inspection checklist. Use the same structure for every unit. When you are back at your desk, use the ⌘ ⇧ 4 shortcut to take screenshots of specific areas if you need to attach them to an email. Keep your folders organized by property name and date. Use Finder tags to label inspection photos as 'Pending' or 'Resolved'.

faq.question: How do I organize inspection photos on my Mac?
faq.answer: Create a dedicated folder for each property. Use the date in the filename, such as 2026-11-05_Unit101. Then use Finder tags to mark them by status.

faq.question: Can I automate my inspection reports?
faq.answer: Yes, by using cloud-based platforms like Buildium or AppFolio that have built-in inspection modules. These sync directly to your dashboard.
